name: Tinder Elo

lead: Tinder Elo is the belief that the dating app assigns each profile a hidden desirability score, modelled on the Elo rating used in chess, and shows profiles to people with similar scores. Within looksmaxxing communities it is a way of thinking about why some profiles get many matches and others few.

The appearance payoff comes through photos and presentation: if better pictures draw more right swipes from desirable users, the score is said to rise. Tinder's CEO described an Elo-style score in 2016 reporting, and the company said in 2019 that it no longer relies on Elo.

paras: Community methods include making a fresh account, limiting swiping sessions, being selective about right swipes, switching settings between searches, and using new, higher-quality photos. Forum members disagree on whether any of these change outcomes.

There is little physical risk. Reported downsides are time spent, disappointment when methods do not change match counts, and privacy considerations when using VPNs or multiple accounts, which can conflict with app terms.

angle.text: Forum users treat the supposed score as a reason to improve photos, grooming and swiping habits, expecting better profiles to be shown more often. How Tinder ranks profiles today is not published in detail.

lead: Tinder Elo is a community term for a supposed hidden attractiveness or desirability score that Tinder uses to decide whose profiles are shown to whom. The name comes from the Elo rating system created by Hungarian-American physicist Arpad Elo to rank chess players, which adjusts a rating up or down depending on the rating of the opponent beaten or lost to.[1]

Looksmaxxers discuss it because it links appearance directly to dating-app visibility: the idea is that photos and swiping behaviour raise or lower the score, so better photos, grooming and presentation lead to being shown to more attractive users and more matches. Looksmax.org threads describe attempts to boost or reset the score.[2][3]

Tinder's chief executive Sean Rad was reported in 2016 as describing an Elo-style desirability score, and in a March 2019 blog post the company said Elo was outdated and no longer used, adding that matching relies on recent activity, preferences and location.[4][4]
infobox: March 2019: Elo no longer relied on

paras: The Elo rating system estimates relative skill: a player's rating rises when they beat a higher-rated opponent and falls when they lose to a lower-rated one. The United States Chess Federation adopted it in 1960 and FIDE in 1970, and it has since been adapted to other competitive settings.[1] Wikipedia notes that dating apps, including Tinder, have been described as using a variant.[1]

In the Tinder version of the theory, being swiped right by people with high scores raises your own, while being swiped left by them lowers it, and profiles are shown mainly to others of similar rank. A looksmax.org method thread describes it as a ranking based on right-swipe proportion and recommends selective swiping and periodic account resets, crediting the technique to a user on another forum.[2]

Secondary reports say that in 2016 Fast Company reported Tinder's CEO describing an Elo score based on desirability.[4] In March 2019 Tinder published a post saying Elo was an outdated measure its technology no longer relies on; it said matching uses recent activity, preferences and location, and that each like or pass can change a profile's recommendations within about 24 hours.[4] Commentators noted that the new system still depends on who swipes on whom and that Tinder did not explain it in detail.[4]

Looksmax.org members hold opposing views. One poster argued that Tinder Elo does not exist, reporting steady matches after swiping only on women he rated highly, and that low matches reflect competition from many attractive men.[3] Others in the same thread replied that the effect becomes visible with longer use.[3] A separate thread asks how to fully reset the score, for example by using a VPN and new account.[5]
The topic overlaps with photo optimisation, since the claimed route to a higher score is a stronger profile.

No studies found. A 2016 study of Tinder use in New York City and London, summarised on Tinder's Wikipedia article, found men liked a large share of profiles but matched about 0.6 percent of the time, while women were more selective and matched at a higher rate.[6]
